title: The Vertigo of Being Promoted Past My Competence
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] There's a particular vertigo that arrives roughly six months into a promotion you privately suspect exceeded your actual capabilities, a suspicion no congratulatory email quite manages to dispel.
Narrator: I'd spent a decade excelling at the discrete, bounded work of an individual contributor, the kind with visible edges and defensible outcomes.
Narrator: [carefully] Leadership, by contrast, offered no such edges, only an amorphous expectation that I somehow metabolize other people's ambiguity into decisions nobody else wanted to own.

Narrator: I performed competence for months, nodding through meetings whose stakes I only half grasped, terrified that admitting confusion would confirm what I already suspected everyone secretly believed.
Narrator: [reflective] The exhaustion of that performance eventually outpaced my capacity to sustain it, which is, I've since realized, precisely how most people finally confess to struggling.
Narrator: I told my own mentor, haltingly, that I thought the promotion had been a mistake, that I'd been elevated past whatever ceiling my actual skill honestly warranted.

Narrator: [honestly] She didn't reassure me, which I initially resented, and instead asked a question I hadn't thought to ask myself: whether competence at this level even resembled competence at the last one.
Narrator: It doesn't, I slowly understood. The very qualities that had made me exceptional before, precision, individual ownership, a taste for solving things alone, actively undermined me now.
Narrator: [gently] What this role actually demanded was closer to translation than execution: absorbing chaos from a dozen directions and returning something coherent enough for others to act on.
Narrator: So I stopped measuring myself against my old competence entirely, and began, awkwardly, building the unfamiliar muscles this altogether different job actually required.
Narrator: [calmly] The vertigo hasn't disappeared completely, and I suspect it never fully will, each new altitude apparently arriving with its own particular thinness of air.
Narrator: But I've stopped mistaking that thinness for proof I don't belong here, and started treating it, instead, as the unglamorous, ordinary texture of actually growing.

quiz.question: When does the narrator say this vertigo typically arrives?
options: Roughly six months into a promotion he privately suspects exceeded his capabilities
Immediately after the promotion
Only on his last day
Before the promotion was even announced
quiz.explanation: He says the vertigo arrives about six months in, once the initial congratulations fade.

quiz.question: What kind of work had the narrator excelled at previously?
options: Vague, unstructured leadership tasks
Discrete, bounded individual-contributor work with visible edges and defensible outcomes
Public speaking engagements
Managing large teams
quiz.explanation: He had excelled at bounded individual-contributor work with clear edges, unlike the ambiguity of leadership.

quiz.question: What question did his mentor ask instead of reassuring him?
options: Whether he wanted to quit
Whether he had asked for a raise
Whether competence at this level even resembled competence at the last one
Whether his team liked him
quiz.explanation: His mentor asked whether competence at his new level even resembled competence at his previous one, prompting reflection.

quiz.question: What did the narrator realize his old strengths did in the new role?
options: They transferred perfectly
They were completely irrelevant either way
They made the promotion easier
They actively undermined him, since the role demanded different qualities
quiz.explanation: He realized the precision and solo focus that once made him excellent now actively undermined him in the new role.

quiz.question: How does the narrator ultimately interpret the persistent 'thinness of air'?
options: As the unglamorous, ordinary texture of actually growing
As proof he doesn't belong in the role
As a sign he should resign immediately
As something that will vanish completely soon
quiz.explanation: He stops treating the vertigo as proof of not belonging and instead treats it as the ordinary texture of growth.

quiz.question: What central claim does “The Vertigo of Being Promoted Past My Competence” develop?
options: Automation can change a role without erasing responsibility for workers.
Promotion can expose limits that require support, not concealment.
Craft can survive automation when judgment remains accountable.
Honest exit feedback can reveal process failure without retaliation.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s evidence, accountability, and proportionate repair.

quiz.question: Which evidence best supports the reasoning in “The Vertigo of Being Promoted Past My Competence”?
options: The narrator’s redundancy follows a system he helped create.
Editors distinguish speed from editorial responsibility.
Vertigo follows responsibility beyond familiar competence.
The interview makes room for evidence about recurring conditions.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s evidence, accountability, and proportionate repair.

quiz.question: Which qualification limits the inference in “The Vertigo of Being Promoted Past My Competence”?
options: Efficiency gains do not settle questions of fair transition.
A tool’s output is not evidence of its suitability.
One report does not prove every allegation or motive.
Confidence is not proof that a decision is sound.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s evidence, accountability, and proportionate repair.

quiz.question: Which response best expresses the speaker’s stance in “The Vertigo of Being Promoted Past My Competence”?
options: The narrator seeks evidence and help before acting.
He reports impacts rather than claiming intent for decision-makers.
They test claims against readers and consequences.
The organisation should investigate proportionately and protect reporting routes.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s evidence, accountability, and proportionate repair.

quiz.question: What implication follows most clearly from “The Vertigo of Being Promoted Past My Competence”?
options: Accountable innovation includes repair for displaced people.
Accountability includes naming scope and escalation needs.
Human oversight matters when choices shape meaning.
Repair requires more than collecting uncomfortable feedback.
quiz.explanation: The answer follows from the account’s evidence, accountability, and proportionate repair.
